Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
Any form of physical contact with others

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

I am permanently an outsider now
People are not what they seem

issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is only partly coherent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. Nausea and visible injuries fit partner physical abuse, but darkness is a more context-specific trigger that is not supported by the memory or appraisal items; no item suggests assaults occurring in dark spaces or fear linked to darkness specifically.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is hard to explain from the rest of the profile. None of the trigger, memory, or appraisal items point to buses/trains/crowds/public transit as trauma-linked cues, so this strategy appears to target a symptom context not otherwise represented in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner,' the trigger 'being alone with men' is hard to reconcile unless the abusive partner was male and the fear generalized specifically to men; demographics/trauma description do not support that specificity, so this item is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'People can't be trusted' is very broad and non-specific, while the trigger pattern is specifically male-coded. That combination is not impossible, but here it weakens coherence because the profile gives no corresponding trauma-linked reason for a male-specific trigger alongside a fully generalized interpersonal belief.

Within the Memory node, 'hard to deliberately recall' and 'memories are very clear and detailed' can coexist in PTSD, but in this profile they are phrased in a way that risks direct contradiction unless the distinction between involuntary vivid intrusions and impaired voluntary recall is explicit. A clinician would likely question whether these two items were selected to describe the same memory pattern without additional clarification.

vignette: Ryan had always been a man of action, with a sharp mind and a quick wit that served him well in his work as a detective. But it was his personal life that had once brought him joy, not his job. He had met his wife, Emily, in college, and they had been inseparable ever since. Or so he thought. It started with small things - a slammed door, a raised voice, a careless comment that cut deep. Ryan tried to brush it off as stress or fatigue, but the incidents piled up, each one leaving him feeling more and more on edge. And then there was the night it all escalated into physical abuse. Emily's face had been twisted in rage, her eyes blazing with a fury he'd never seen before. He remembered the sound of his own voice, pleading with her to stop, as she slammed her fist into his jaw. The months that followed were a blur of pain and fear. Ryan couldn't shake the memories of that night - the feeling of being trapped, helpless, and alone. The sounds still echoed in his head - Emily's labored breathing, the creaking of the floorboards beneath their feet. He'd catch himself replaying the scene over and over, as if trying to make sense of it all. As a detective, Ryan was used to dealing with violence and trauma on a daily basis, but this was different. This was personal. He started to avoid relaxing, afraid that letting his guard down would leave him vulnerable again. He became withdrawn, numbing his feelings to the point where even his wife's touch felt like a threat. Simple things triggered him now - the smell of alcohol wafting from a passing stranger, a glimpse of someone else's injuries on the news. His stomach would churn with nausea, and he'd feel himself transported back to that terrible night. He couldn't bear the thought of being touched, not even by his wife. Physical contact felt like an invasion, a breach of his fragile defenses. Ryan started to pull away from Emily, using work as an excuse to avoid intimacy. She sensed something was wrong but couldn't quite put her finger on it. Their conversations grew stilted, and their relationship began to fray at the edges. As Ryan's world shrunk, he found himself increasingly isolated. He'd always prided himself on his ability to read people, to know when someone was hiding something. But now everyone seemed like a potential threat - even Emily. He couldn't shake the feeling that she was just waiting for him to let his guard down again. Ryan lost faith in everything - people, life, the whole notion of justice. The world felt like a dark and twisted place, full of predators lurking in every shadow. His memories of that night were still raw, refusing to be buried. They'd surface at odd moments, forcing their way into his mind like an uninvited guest. It was only when he found himself snapping at a colleague, lashing out for no reason, that Ryan realized something had to change. He couldn't keep living in this state of hyper-vigilance, constantly on edge and waiting for the next blow to fall. The pain and fear were suffocating him, eating away at his very sense of self. With a heavy heart, Ryan made an appointment with a therapist, hoping against hope that someone could help him untangle the mess in his head. As he sat in the waiting room, flipping through a worn copy of People magazine, he felt a glimmer of trepidation. What if this didn't work? What if he was forever trapped in this cycle of fear and mistrust? But as he stood up to greet the therapist, Ryan knew he had no choice but to try. He couldn't keep living like this - lost, alone, and perpetually on edge. For the first time in months, he allowed himself a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, there was a way out of this darkness after all.
